Trying to Conceive

One or two embryos? Understanding the transfer decision

Updated: November 11, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

When several embryos are available, transferring more at once can feel like taking a stronger chance. The decision is more complicated: a higher chance from one procedure can come with a much higher chance of twins, while separate single transfers may preserve a useful cumulative opportunity. The aim is a healthy birth with the least avoidable risk, using a plan that fits your embryos and medical circumstances.

One transfer and a treatment strategy are different comparisons

Elective single-embryo transfer means choosing one embryo when more than one suitable embryo is available. Other suitable embryos may be stored for later use. If only one is available, transferring it is also a single transfer, but there is no choice between one and several. Double-embryo transfer puts two embryos into the uterus during the same procedure.

Compare two plans clearly: transferring two together, or transferring one and considering another later if needed. The second plan may involve another appointment, monitoring and expense. It also allows each embryo a separate opportunity without deliberately exposing the same pregnancy to two implanting embryos. Neither plan guarantees implantation, a continuing pregnancy or a baby.

Ask what a success percentage actually measures

Implantation describes an early event, often reported per embryo transferred. A positive pregnancy test, an ultrasound-confirmed pregnancy and a live birth are different outcomes. A percentage of embryos that implant cannot be read as the percentage of patients who take home a baby. Nor can a clinic simply double a single-transfer percentage to predict the chance from transferring two.

For this decision, request live-birth results for comparable patients and ask whether they cover one transfer or successive transfers from the same collection. Ask how many patients were included and whether people who never reached a later transfer were counted. Cumulative results need a defined period and treatment pathway. Age-band figures without a date, denominator or patient description are too incomplete to guide your choice.

What randomized evidence says about successive single transfers

In a 2004 randomized trial, women younger than 36 with at least two good-quality embryos received either two fresh embryos together or one fresh embryo followed, if needed, by one frozen embryo. Live birth occurred in about 43% of the double-transfer group and 39% of the successive-single group. Multiple births were much less frequent with the single-transfer strategy. The trial did not establish equivalence under its prespecified statistical margin, so it should not be described as proving identical success.

A 2020 Cochrane review found that repeated single transfers may produce a cumulative live-birth chance similar to one double transfer while reducing multiple pregnancy. The cumulative evidence came from four studies with 985 participants and was of low certainty for live birth. Most participants were younger and had a good prognosis, and these comparisons used cleavage-stage embryos. The findings support discussing the whole strategy, while leaving uncertainty for other patient groups.

Newer registry studies add context, not a personal prediction

A 2025 UK registry study examined more than 71,000 women undergoing their first egg collection with blastocyst transfer. Two consecutive single transfers were associated with comparable or better live-birth outcomes and fewer adverse outcomes than double transfer. However, the database lacked some important information, including embryo quality and body mass index. Patients were not randomly assigned to their transfer strategy, so differences between groups may have influenced the results.

A 2026 German registry analysis also distinguished one attempt from a sequence. One double transfer had a higher live-birth rate than one single transfer, but two successive single transfers had a higher cumulative rate than one double transfer, with fewer multiple births. This was a matched observational analysis, not a randomized trial. Together, these studies reinforce why “better per transfer” and “better over a treatment plan” are not interchangeable claims.

Why avoiding a multiple pregnancy matters

Transferring two embryos can result in no pregnancy, one developing baby or more than one; the outcome cannot be chosen after transfer. A twin pregnancy brings more medical risk than a singleton pregnancy, including preterm birth, low birth weight and admission to neonatal care. The pregnant person also faces higher risks of complications such as pre-eclampsia and gestational diabetes. These are reasons to prevent avoidable multiple pregnancy, not a judgment about families with twins.

A single embryo can occasionally divide and produce identical twins. Choosing one therefore reduces multiple-pregnancy risk substantially without making it zero. Transferring more embryos is not a reliable way to complete a family in one pregnancy. Discuss the chance of a healthy birth alongside the number of babies, and ask which maternal and infant outcomes are included in the clinic’s figures.

Age matters, but it does not decide the number by itself

The age of the person who provided the eggs at collection is relevant to embryo prognosis. For donor eggs, the donor’s age is the egg-age reference; for stored embryos, a later birthday does not change the age at which the eggs were obtained. The current health of the person carrying the pregnancy still matters, especially if a multiple pregnancy would add substantial medical risk.

Ask the clinic to explain the combination of factors behind its recommendation: egg age, embryo development, available embryos, previous treatment and your medical circumstances. A poor outcome in an earlier cycle does not show that transferring two would have prevented it. ESHRE advises against using age or previous unsuccessful treatment alone as the reason for double transfer. More complex circumstances deserve an individual explanation of both uncertainty and risk.

Embryo appearance and genetic testing answer different questions

Laboratory grading describes features seen as an embryo develops, such as cell characteristics and, at the blastocyst stage, the appearance of different cell groups. It helps rank embryos for potential use. A good-looking embryo is not proof that every chromosome is normal, and a lower grade is not the same as no chance of a baby. Ask what the grade means in the laboratory that assessed your embryos.

PGT-A is a separate test of chromosome number in sampled cells. It does not repair an embryo or guarantee a healthy child. HFEA finds no randomized-trial evidence that it improves the chance of a baby for most IVF patients; biopsy, inaccurate results and loss of potentially usable embryos are relevant limitations. A result reported as euploid is not a reason to transfer several: ASRM recommends one euploid embryo regardless of age.

Guideline limits are not numbers to aim for

ASRM’s 2021 guidance sets upper limits that vary with age, embryo stage and prognosis, while aiming for a healthy singleton pregnancy. Some circumstances permit more than one untested embryo; this does not mean that using the maximum is the preferred option. The guidance calls for one embryo when a coexisting medical condition makes multiple pregnancy especially hazardous. A clinic should explain any individualized departure from its usual recommendation.

ESHRE’s 2023 guideline, summarized in 2024, more broadly recommends elective single transfer and does not treat an individual clinical or embryo factor as sufficient reason for two. Much of the supporting evidence is low or very low certainty. These documents differ in how they frame exceptions; neither is a universal promise of success. Ask which guidance and local requirements apply, and what evidence supports the recommendation for your combination of circumstances.

Plan what would happen to the remaining embryos

A single-transfer plan is more useful when you understand the next step. Ask whether other embryos are suitable for storage, what future treatment would involve and how a later attempt would be scheduled if the first does not lead to a baby. Not every embryo will reach the stage required for storage or remain suitable after warming. The estimated opportunity from a sequence must reflect those possibilities.

Embryo stage, freezing and the number transferred are related but separate decisions. A frozen transfer is not automatically a reason to transfer more embryos. Keep the consultation focused enough to obtain a clear answer to each question: why this embryo, why this number and why this timing? Ask for the plan in writing if several choices are being discussed at once.

Make room for financial and emotional pressures

After a long wait or an unsuccessful cycle, wanting the greatest possible chance immediately is understandable. Limited funding, travel and time away from work can make another transfer feel difficult. Tell the clinic about those constraints before the transfer day. Request separate estimates for one double transfer and a possible sequence of single transfers, including storage and later monitoring, rather than assuming that the first quoted price represents the whole course.

Ask what counselling or treatment-planning support is available if you feel rushed or disagree with the recommendation. A useful conversation should make the trade-offs visible without suggesting that accepting more risk proves commitment to parenthood. If you already have a multiple pregnancy, this is a reason to arrange appropriate pregnancy care, not to blame yourself for an earlier decision.

Leave the consultation with an explanation you can repeat

Try summarizing the plan back to the team: the proposed number, the main reason for it, the estimated live-birth chance over the agreed pathway and the multiple-pregnancy risk. Ask whether the estimate comes from patients similar to you, and what would change the recommendation on the day. If the explanation rests only on “more embryos means more chance,” ask for the comparison with successive single transfers.

Do not use a general age table or an online success story to choose the number on your own. The final decision needs informed discussion with your fertility team and a clear consent process. Choosing one embryo can be an active way to reduce avoidable risk while preserving later options; it is not a promise that treatment will work or that a further transfer will be available.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Randomized evidence distinguishes a single attempt from repeated single transfers. Cumulative live-birth findings have uncertainty and should not be presented as proof of identical success for every age or embryo type.

The 2025 UK and 2026 German registry analyses provide newer observations about successive transfers. They are not randomized comparisons and cannot remove the possibility that patient or embryo differences influenced outcomes.

ASRM and ESHRE favour reducing multiple pregnancy but frame individual exceptions differently. Discuss the applicable guidance without treating an upper limit as a treatment target.

How BeMama can help

Use these questions to make the proposed embryo-number decision understandable. Your fertility team should relate the evidence to your own embryos, health, priorities and realistic next steps.

When to seek help

Do not select the number of embryos from an online percentage or change treatment plans on your own. Tell the team about medical conditions that could make a multiple pregnancy especially risky, and obtain a clear explanation before consent.

Evidence notes updated: November 11, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Compare successive single transfers with one double transfer, not only one procedure with another.
  • Ask for live-birth and multiple-pregnancy outcomes with clear patient groups and denominators.
  • Egg age, embryo stage and health matter, but no single factor sets a universal number.
  • Embryo grading and PGT-A are different assessments; neither guarantees a baby.
  • Discuss the next-transfer plan, costs and uncertainty before giving consent.

Frequently asked questions

How does IVF success change with age?

Egg-provider age at collection affects prognosis, but an age band alone does not give a personal live-birth chance. Ask for current results in comparable patients, distinguishing implantation from live birth and one transfer from a sequence.

Does transferring more embryos increase implantation?

More embryos do not improve the quality of each embryo, and their probabilities cannot simply be added. Two may increase the chance of a birth from one procedure in some settings, while also increasing multiple pregnancy. Compare that with the cumulative opportunity from separate single transfers.

Is transferring one embryo better than transferring several?

Single transfer is preferred for many patients because it reduces multiple-pregnancy risk. The recommendation should account for your embryos, health and applicable guidance. Guideline ceilings are not targets, and evidence about one attempt is different from evidence about successive attempts.

Is an IVF twin pregnancy a good treatment goal?

Twins can bring joy, but deliberately increasing the chance of twins also increases medical risks. Fertility care generally aims for a healthy singleton birth. If you are already pregnant with twins, seek the recommended pregnancy care and support without blaming yourself.

Can a single embryo produce twins?

Yes. One embryo can split and result in identical twins. Single transfer substantially reduces the risk of multiples but does not eliminate it.

Does a failed transfer mean two should be used next time?

Not by itself. Review the previous cycle and current embryos with the team. ESHRE does not recommend using previous unsuccessful attempts alone as the reason for double transfer.

Should two embryos reported as euploid be transferred together?

ASRM recommends transfer of one euploid embryo regardless of age. PGT-A does not remove the risks of a multiple pregnancy or guarantee a healthy baby. Ask the clinic to explain any proposed alternative.

Does choosing one mean losing the other embryos?

Not necessarily. Other suitable embryos can often be stored for later use. Ask which are suitable, what storage and future transfer involve, and what happens if no embryo remains suitable when another attempt is planned.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
